question.text: If Ms. Priya Shah halves the desired margin of error (from 5% to 2.5%) in her beneficiary sampling plan while keeping p=0.5 and 95% confidence constant, the required sample size will:

explanation.text: The Logic: The standard sample-size formula for estimating a proportion is n = z² x p x (1-p) / e². Here z (for 95% confidence) and p (= 0.5) are held constant, so n scales as 1 / e². If the margin of error e is halved (5% -> 2.5%), then e² becomes one-quarter of its original value, so n becomes four times larger. Starting from n ≈ 385 at e = 5%, halving e to 2.5% gives n ≈ 385 x 4 ≈ 1,540 (≈ 1,537 with exact rounding). Tighter precision is therefore disproportionately expensive in terms of sample size. The Trap: Halving n misreads the relationship - smaller margin of error needs more, not fewer, observations. Staying the same ignores e entirely. Doubling n misses the quadratic (1 / e²) dependence and treats it as linear in 1 / e. Only the quadrupling answer correctly applies the 1 / e² scaling implied by the formula. Note: The cited workbook page (131 of the Social Impact Assessors Certification Examination Workbook) states that a statistically significant sample size requires defining a confidence interval and a margin of error, but it does not present the n = z²·p·(1-p)/e² formula or the halve-error-quadruples-sample-size relationship. The framing above reflects standard statistics / sampling-theory practice used in survey design and audit / beneficiary sampling.
